title: RamanOmics Maps Spatial Vibrational‑Molecular Architecture of Cellular Senescence in Aging and Repair
body:
A new multimodal approach that fuses label‑free Raman spectroscopy with spatially resolved transcriptomics has revealed a distinct biochemical fingerprint of senescent cells in mouse lungs, offering a powerful tool for mapping ageing and tissue repair at single‑cell resolution. The technique, dubbed “RamanOmics,” uncovers a lipid‑associated Raman signature that correlates with the expression of the cell‑cycle inhibitor p21, a hallmark of cellular senescence, and demonstrates how senescent cells remodel their molecular environment during both chronic ageing and acute injury‑driven regeneration.

The research team, led by scientists Zhang, Chen, Monticolo and Sorrentino, applied high‑resolution Raman imaging to fresh frozen sections of mouse lung tissue, capturing vibrational spectra that reflect the composition of proteins, nucleic acids, lipids and metabolites without any fluorescent or antibody labels. Parallel to this, they performed spatial transcriptomics on adjacent sections, generating gene‑expression maps that pinpointed cells expressing senescence‑associated markers such as Cdkn1a (p21) and SASP (senescence‑associated secretory phenotype) factors. By co‑registering the two data sets, the investigators could directly link spectral features to transcriptional programs in individual cells.

The most striking finding was a reproducible Raman band around 2850 cm⁻¹, attributed to CH₂ stretching vibrations in saturated fatty acids, that was consistently enriched in p21⁺ cells across multiple experimental conditions. This lipid‑linked signature persisted in aged lungs, where senescent cells accumulate, as well as in lungs undergoing repair after bleomycin‑induced injury, suggesting that senescent cells adopt a characteristic lipid remodeling that may influence their secretory behavior and interaction with the extracellular matrix. Importantly, the Raman signature was detectable even when p21 expression was low, indicating that RamanOmics can flag senescent cells that might escape conventional immunostaining.

Beyond the immediate discovery, the study showcases the broader potential of integrating vibrational spectroscopy with spatial omics. Traditional methods for identifying senescence rely on immunohistochemistry or bulk RNA sequencing, both of which either lack spatial context or require destructive processing. Raman imaging, by contrast, preserves tissue architecture and can be performed rapidly on unstained sections, making it compatible with clinical pathology workflows. When combined with transcriptomic maps, it enables researchers to interrogate how metabolic shifts—such as lipid accumulation—co‑occur with gene‑regulatory changes, opening avenues to dissect the heterogeneity of senescent populations in vivo.

The implications for ageing research and regenerative medicine are significant. Senescent cells are increasingly recognized as drivers of age‑related dysfunction and as obstacles to effective tissue repair. Therapies that selectively eliminate or reprogram senescent cells—so‑called senolytics and senomorphics—are under intense investigation, yet reliable biomarkers to monitor treatment efficacy remain scarce. RamanOmics could provide a non‑invasive read‑out of senescent burden, allowing longitudinal studies of drug response in animal models and, eventually, in patient biopsies. Moreover, the lipid‑focused Raman signature hints at metabolic vulnerabilities that could be exploited pharmacologically; targeting lipid synthesis or remodeling pathways might blunt the deleterious effects of senescent cells without killing them outright.

Looking ahead, the researchers plan to extend RamanOmics to other organs and disease models, including fibrotic liver and neurodegenerative brain tissue, where senescence also plays a pivotal role. Scaling the technique to larger tissue volumes and integrating it with emerging spatial proteomics platforms could further enrich the molecular portrait of ageing cells. As the field moves toward comprehensive, multimodal atlases of the human body, tools that bridge chemistry and genomics—like RamanOmics—will be essential for translating molecular insights into therapeutic strategies that mitigate the impacts of ageing and promote healthier tissue regeneration.
